title: List-endpoint & write-endpoint logic
description: The logic layer of every CRUD interview exercise, as pure functions: page envelopes, defensive parameter clamping, sort-field whitelists, optional (null = not sent) filters, opaque cursor tokens, ETag / If-Match preconditions, idempotent PUT upserts and JSON-merge-patch semantics (RFC 7386: null deletes) on plain dictionaries. Nearest existing units: jstrain-cs 04/04 (Skip/Take paging mechanics) and 27/02 (offset-vs-keyset drift) — here only the envelope and token mechanics; jstrain-cs 16/* (DataAnnotations validation), 28/* (retry / circuit breaker) and 11/* (System.Text.Json — 10/08 merges dictionaries, no serializer).

exercises.title: Page envelope: totalPages and hasNext
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The list endpoint returns 95 items at 10 per page — how many pages, and does page 10 have a next?"

**Contract.** `TotalPages` is a ceiling division with one special case: zero items is zero pages (an empty collection has no page 1). `HasNext(page, …)` is true exactly while `page` is below the total page count. Integer math only — no doubles.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `int TotalPages(int totalItems, int pageSize)` → `0` when `totalItems == 0`, else `(totalItems + pageSize - 1) / pageSize`
- `bool HasNext(int page, int totalItems, int pageSize)` → `page < TotalPages(totalItems, pageSize)`

**Worked example.** 95 items at 10/page → (95 + 9) / 10 = **10 pages**; page 10 has no next, page 1 does.
exercises.explanation:
Ceiling division without floats: adding `pageSize - 1` before the integer divide bumps any partial page up to a whole one.

For `TotalPages(95, 10)`:
- 95 + 9 = 104; 104 / 10 (integer) = **10 pages**
- 100 items stays 10 (109 / 10 = 10) — an exact fit must NOT create an empty page 11
- 0 items short-circuits to **0** — an empty collection has no page 1

`HasNext` is then one comparison. Returning `totalPages` and `hasNext` beside the rows is what lets a client render a pager without a second COUNT round-trip.
hints: Integer division truncates toward zero, which rounds partial pages DOWN — you want them rounded up.
ceil(a / b) for positive ints = (a + b − 1) / b in integer math; zero items is a special case.
Add pageSize minus one to the item count before the integer divide, special-casing zero items to zero pages — a next page exists while the page number is below the total page count

exercises.title: Clamp paging parameters
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Your list endpoint takes `page` and `pageSize` from the query string. What do you do with `pageSize=0`, `pageSize=250000` and `page=0`?"

**Contract.**
- `ClampPageSize`: a non-positive request means "not sent" → `fallback`; anything above `max` → `max` (an unbounded page size is a denial-of-service lever); otherwise the request as-is.
- `OffsetOf`: pages are **1-based**; a page below 1 is treated as page 1; the row offset is `(page - 1) * pageSize`.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `int ClampPageSize(int requested, int fallback, int max)`
- `int OffsetOf(int page, int pageSize)`

**Worked example.** `OffsetOf(3, 20)` → pages 1 and 2 cover 40 rows → **40**.
exercises.explanation:
Parameter clamping is the first line of an endpoint: normalize, then compute.

For `ClampPageSize(250, 20, 100)`:
- 250 > 0, so not "missing"
- 250 > 100 → **100**

`OffsetOf(0, 20)`: page 0 is floored to 1 → (1 − 1) × 20 = **0**. Clamping instead of rejecting keeps old or sloppy clients working while still bounding the database's work.
hints: Two different bad inputs need two different answers: "missing" falls back to the default, "too big" is cut to the ceiling.
requested <= 0 ? fallback : Math.Min(requested, max); offset = (Math.Max(page, 1) - 1) * pageSize.
Treat non-positive sizes as the default and anything above the ceiling as the ceiling, then compute the offset from a page number floored at one so page one always starts at zero

exercises.title: Sort through a whitelist
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Add `?sort=` to the users endpoint. A teammate wrote `ORDER BY {sort}`. Fix it."

**Contract.**
- `ParseSort`: `null` or `""` → `(fallback, false)`. A leading `-` means descending and the rest is the field; otherwise ascending. A bare `"-"` (no field after the minus) is junk → `(fallback, false)`.
- `MapSort`: the API field is looked up case-insensitively — compare `field.ToLowerInvariant()` against the dictionary's lowercase keys — and translated to its real column. A field the whitelist does not name → `fallbackColumn`. User text never becomes SQL; only whitelist VALUES do.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `(string Field, bool Desc) ParseSort(string? requested, string fallback)`
- `string MapSort(string field, Dictionary<string, string> allowed, string fallbackColumn)`

**Worked example.** `"-name"` → `("name", true)` → `MapSort("name", {name: "u.name", …}, "u.id")` → **`ORDER BY u.name DESC`**.
exercises.explanation:
Parsing and mapping are separate steps: the first decodes the client's syntax, the second decides what is allowed to touch the database.

For `ParseSort("-", "id")`:
- not null/empty; first char is `-` → desc = true, field = `""`
- an empty field is meaningless → **`("id", false)`**

`MapSort("password", …)` → no such key → `"u.id"`: an attacker can choose among your sort columns and nothing else — which is the entire defense against ORDER BY injection.
hints: Split the job: first decode "-field" into a field and a direction, then decide which real column (if any) that field may become.
requested[0] == '-' → desc, field = requested[1..]; allowed.TryGetValue(field.ToLowerInvariant(), out var col) ? col : fallbackColumn.

Strip an optional leading minus to learn the direction, then translate the remaining word through a known-fields dictionary case-insensitively, answering the safe fallback column for anything the whitelist does not name

exercises.title: Optional filters: null means not sent
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The products endpoint takes three optional filters. Write the filtering so that leaving a filter out never hides products."

**Contract.** Each criterion applies **only when its argument is non-null**; a `null` argument means the client did not send that filter and admits every item. Present criteria combine with AND.
- `nameContains`: `Name.Contains(nameContains, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`
- `maxPriceCents`: `PriceCents <= max` (inclusive)
- `active`: `Active == active` — note `false` is a real filter value, not "absent"
Input order is preserved.

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `List<(string Name, int PriceCents, bool Active)> Apply(items, string? nameContains, int? maxPriceCents, bool? active)`

**Worked example.** Items Red Mug (900, active), Blue Mug (1100, active), Red Cap (700, inactive); `maxPriceCents = 900` → **[Red Mug, Red Cap]**.
exercises.explanation:
Build the query up conditionally: start from everything and narrow once per filter that was actually sent.

For `Apply(items, "red", 800, true)`:
- name contains "red" → Red Mug, Red Cap
- price ≤ 800 → Red Cap (Red Mug is 900)
- active == true → Red Cap is inactive → **[]**

The classic bug is treating `active = false` as "not sent" (`if (active == true)`); a `bool?` keeps the three states — yes, no, don't care — distinct.
hints: A missing filter must not exclude anything, so each criterion is conditional on its argument being present.
Start with IEnumerable q = items; if (nameContains is not null) q = q.Where(...); same for maxPriceCents is int max and active is bool a.
Apply each criterion only when its nullable argument carries a value, chaining them as and-conditions, so an absent filter admits everything and present filters conjoin

exercises.title: Opaque cursor tokens
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We're moving `/events` from offset to keyset pagination. Design the `next` cursor the client echoes back — and tell me what happens when someone sends garbage."

**Contract.**
- `EncodeCursor`: the last row's id as invariant-culture decimal text, UTF-8 encoded, then Base64 — opaque to the client (they must echo it, not compute it).
- `DecodeCursor`: `null` or `""` → `null` (first page). Invalid Base64 → `null` (catch the `FormatException`). Decoded text that is not an integer (`long.TryParse` with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`) → `null`. Otherwise the id. It never throws.
- The id travels as a STRING, so 64-bit ids survive JavaScript clients (which lose precision above 2^53).

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `string EncodeCursor(long lastId)`
- `long? DecodeCursor(string? token)`

**Worked example.** `EncodeCursor(42)` → text `"42"` → bytes `34 32` → **`NDI=`**.
exercises.explanation:
The cursor is a tiny serialization format, so decoding it has every failure mode of parsing: bad envelope (Base64), bad payload (not a number), or missing.

For `DecodeCursor("NDI=")`:
- not empty → Base64 decodes to bytes `34 32` → UTF-8 text `"42"`
- `long.TryParse("42", …)` succeeds → **42**

`DecodeCursor("!!!")` hits the `FormatException` branch and returns `null`; the endpoint answers 400 or restarts from page one, but never 500 because a client edited a URL.
hints: Encoding is the easy direction; decoding has three distinct ways to fail and each must become null rather than an exception.
Convert.ToBase64String(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(id.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture))); decode with try/catch (FormatException) then long.TryParse(…, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var id).
Encode the invariant decimal text of the id as base64 for an opaque token, and decode defensively, translating bad base64 or non-numeric content into null instead of an exception

exercises.title: ETag and If-Match preconditions
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Two support agents open the same ticket, both edit, both save. How does your PUT endpoint stop the second save from erasing the first?"

**Contract.**
- `ETagOf(version)` → `"v{version}"` **including the double quotes** — they are part of the ETag grammar (`ETagOf(3)` is the 4-character string `"v3"`).
- `PreconditionHolds(ifMatch, etag)`: this endpoint REQUIRES `If-Match`, so a missing header (`null`) fails closed; `"*"` matches any existing representation; otherwise exact, case-sensitive string equality.
- `StatusFor(exists, holds)`: check existence first — not found → **404**; found but the precondition failed → **412 Precondition Failed**; otherwise the write happens → **204 No Content**.

**Your task.** Implement the three stubbed local functions:
- `string ETagOf(int version)`
- `bool PreconditionHolds(string? ifMatch, string etag)`
- `int StatusFor(bool exists, bool preconditionHolds)`

**Worked example.** The record is at version 3 (`"v3"`); a client that read version 2 sends `If-Match: "v2"` → precondition fails → **412**.
exercises.explanation:
Optimistic concurrency over HTTP: the client proves which version it edited, and the server refuses the write if that is no longer current.

For a client holding `"v2"` against a record now at `"v3"`:
- `PreconditionHolds("\"v2\"", "\"v3\"")` → not `*`, not equal → false
- `StatusFor(true, false)` → exists, precondition failed → **412**

The client must re-GET, merge, and retry with the new tag. Making `If-Match` mandatory (null → false) is what turns lost-update protection from opt-in into a guarantee.
hints: The server compares the version the client edited against the current one; decide separately what a missing header and the wildcard mean.
$"\"v{version}\""; null → false, "*" → true, else ifMatch == etag; status: 404 before 412 before 204.

Quote the version to form the entity tag, demand an If-Match where a missing header fails closed and a star succeeds, and map the three outcomes to not-found, precondition-failed and no-content in that order of checks

exercises.title: Idempotent PUT upsert
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Implement `PUT /items/{id}`. A mobile client retries every request on a flaky network — what does the second identical PUT do, and which status codes do the two calls return?"

**Contract.** `Upsert` writes `body` under `id` in `store` (mutating it in place) and returns `true` when the id did not exist before (created), `false` when an existing value was replaced. PUT is **idempotent**: replaying an identical request leaves the store exactly as one request did (it is a replace, reported as `false`). `StatusForUpsert` maps created → **201**, replaced → **200**.

**Your task.** Implement the two stubbed local functions:
- `bool Upsert(Dictionary<string, string> store, string id, string body)`
- `int StatusForUpsert(bool created)`

**Worked example.** Empty store; `Upsert(store, "a", "v1")` → **true** (201); the same call again → **false** (200), store still `{ a: "v1" }`.
exercises.explanation:
PUT is "make the resource at this URL equal to this body" — the same assignment whether or not it existed; only the response differs.

For two identical `Upsert(store, "a", "v1")` calls on an empty store:
- first: `"a"` absent → created = true; `store["a"] = "v1"` → **201**
- second: `"a"` present → created = false; same assignment, same state → **200**

Contrast POST-to-collection, where a retry creates a duplicate — that is why idempotency keys exist for POST and not for PUT.
hints: Created-versus-replaced is a fact about the store BEFORE the write; the write itself is identical either way.
created = !store.ContainsKey(id); store[id] = body; return created — and created ? 201 : 200.
Whether the key already exists decides created versus replaced, the write itself is the same assignment either way, and replaying an identical request must leave the store byte-for-byte as it was

exercises.title: JSON merge patch on a dictionary
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our PATCH endpoint follows JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386). The client sends `{"nickname": null}`. What happens to the stored nickname — and to the fields the client didn't mention?"

**Contract.** Working on flat `Dictionary<string, string?>` documents (no serializer): start from a **copy** of `current`, then for each patch entry:
- value `null` → **remove** that key (removing an absent key is a no-op)
- any other value → set the key (overwrite or insert)
Keys the patch never mentions survive untouched. Return the new dictionary; `current` itself must not change (the caller may still need the old version, e.g. for an audit diff).

**Your task.** Implement the stubbed local function:
- `Dictionary<string, string?> Merge(Dictionary<string, string?> current, Dictionary<string, string?> patch)`

**Worked example.** `Merge({a: "1", b: "2"}, {b: null, c: "3"})` → b deleted, c added → **`{a: "1", c: "3"}`**.
exercises.explanation:
Merge patch overloads `null`: in the patch it means "delete", so absent and null are two different instructions — absent keeps, null removes.

For `Merge({a: "1", b: "2"}, {b: null, c: "3"})`:
- copy → `{a: "1", b: "2"}`
- `b: null` → remove b → `{a: "1"}`
- `c: "3"` → set c → **`{a: "1", c: "3"}`**

The corollary interviewers probe: merge patch cannot set a field TO null — if null must be storable, you need JSON Patch (RFC 6902) instead.
hints: In this format "missing" and "null" are two different instructions — and the original document must come out of the call unchanged.
var result = new Dictionary<string, string?>(current); foreach (var (k, v) in patch) if (v is null) result.Remove(k); else result[k] = v.
Start from a copy of the current state, then walk the patch letting a null value remove the key and any other value overwrite or insert it, while keys the patch never mentions survive untouched
